record.paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
record.original_question: What are the size and importance of initial flow—the initial velocity or momentum fields produced before hydrodynamic evolution—and how should the complete energy-momentum tensor, including shear-stress components, be used to initialize hydrodynamic simulations of heavy-ion collisions?

evidence.quote:
Since the initial evolution produces finite initial velocity fields, a complete energy￾momentum tensor including shear stress components should be used to initialize the
hydrodynamic evolution. There are a few studies on the influence of initial flow in the
system, but a consensus on its size and importance has not been reached yet.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In the hydrodynamic modeling of relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the strongly interacting matter formed shortly after the collision is described by relativistic viscous hydrodynamics, governed by conservation of the full energy-momentum tensor T^{μν}, which in the Landau frame decomposes as

  T^{μν} = ε u^μ u^ν − (P + Π) Δ^{μν} + π^{μν},

where ε is the local energy density, u^μ the fluid four-velocity (with u^μ u_μ = 1), Δ^{μν} = g^{μν} − u^μ u^ν the spatial projector, P(ε) the equilibrium pressure, Π the bulk viscous pressure, and π^{μν} the (traceless, transverse) shear-stress tensor. Hydrodynamic simulations require, at some initialization proper time τ_0, specification of the full set of fields (ε, u^μ, π^{μν}, Π).

The pre-equilibrium dynamics preceding hydrodynamization generally produce nonvanishing transverse flow ("initial flow") and nonzero shear-stress components at τ_0, so initial conditions that set u^i = 0 and π^{μν} = 0 are not generic.

Determine, quantitatively, the magnitude and phenomenological importance of the initial transverse velocity / momentum fields generated prior to hydrodynamic evolution, and prescribe how the complete energy-momentum tensor T^{μν}—including its shear-stress components π^{μν} and any nonzero initial flow u^μ—should be constructed and used to initialize relativistic viscous hydrodynamic simulations of heavy-ion collisions, so as to consistently match pre-equilibrium dynamics onto hydrodynamics and yield a definite impact on final-state observables (e.g. anisotropic flow coefficients v_n and their event-by-event correlations).
artifact.status_search_result: Significant progress has been made: QCD kinetic theory frameworks (e.g. KøMPøST) now smoothly match pre-equilibrium evolution onto viscous hydrodynamics, providing consistent initial conditions for ε, u^μ, and π^{μν}, and recent linear-response frameworks (2024) derive estimators using full early-time T^{μν} including momentum-space components. However, a quantitative consensus on the size and phenomenological importance of initial flow across models has not been fully established, so the question is partially solved rather than closed.

status_evidence.title: Matching the Nonequilibrium Initial Stage of Heavy Ion Collisions to Hydrodynamics with QCD Kinetic Theory
status_evidence.snippet: Pre-equilibrium evolution from QCD kinetic theory matches smoothly onto viscous hydrodynamics, providing initial conditions for energy density, flow velocity, and shear stress.
status_evidence.claim: A consistent matching procedure for the full T^{μν} (including initial flow and shear stress) onto hydrodynamics has been developed.

status_evidence.title: Initial energy-momentum to final flow: a general framework for heavy-ion collisions
status_evidence.snippet: New estimators consider the system response to additional aspects of the early-time state, including momentum-space properties encoded in other components of the energy-momentum tensor.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work formalizes how the full initial T^{μν}, including initial flow and shear stress, maps to final-state flow observables.

status_evidence.title: An Initial State with Shear in Peripheral Heavy Ion Collisions
status_evidence.snippet: Large initial angular momentum leads to rotation and fluid shear in the initial state, with large flow vorticity.
status_evidence.claim: Initial flow and shear are non-negligible and impact observables, but their precise size remains model-dependent.
